# **Deep Research Brief: Physically Modeling the Transverse Vibration and Acoustic Articulation of a Helical Spring Doorstop**

## **Executive Diagnosis**

An exhaustive mathematical and acoustic evaluation of the provided ReferenceSpringEngine implementation 1 against the empirical evidence derived from the isolated 81458 helical spring doorstop recording 1 reveals fundamental architectural discrepancies. The existing digital signal processing model successfully generates plausible, tunable acoustic resonators, yet it fundamentally fails to reproduce the recognizable physical object. This failure is not a matter of improper frequency tuning or inadequate modal density, but is instead rooted in the mathematical topology of the macroscopic excitation mechanism and the artificially rapid energy dissipation imposed upon the modal structure.  
The current engine models the macroscopic bending of the spring as a nonlinear continuous oscillator, employing a potential energy formulation defined by a linear stiffness term and a cubic nonlinear stiffness term, expressed as a function of displacement.1 While this Duffing-style polynomial nonlinearity is entirely appropriate for modeling the amplitude-dependent pitch glide of a continuously tensioned beam, it inherently models a smooth, continuous restoring force. Consequently, the coupling between this low-frequency macroscopic motion and the high-frequency modal bank remains continuous and spectrally localized. The empirical recording of the physical doorstop, however, is characterized by a violent, recurring, and periodic articulation—a distinct "boing" consisting of audible energy lobes recurring at approximately ![][image1].1  
These periodic acoustic lobes are generated by high-frequency, broadband impulses injected into the physical system at specific phases of the macroscopic swing. A continuous cubic nonlinearity cannot generate the sharp, broadband energy required to excite high-frequency structural modes at ![][image2], ![][image3], ![][image4], ![][image5], and ![][image6] without artificially over-driving the system, which typically causes numerical instability or unnatural, tinny aliasing artifacts.1 Furthermore, the velocity-limiting algorithm present in the ReferenceSpringEngine utilizes a hyperbolic tangent function to dynamically compress candidate velocities that exceed a predefined kinetic energy knee.1 While this is an excellent safeguard against numerical explosion during bipolar modular synthesis retriggers, it actively suppresses the exact high-acceleration transients required to produce the characteristic broadband sizzle of coil-to-coil impact.  
The decay characteristics of the current model are equally incongruent with the physical object. The empirical measurement of the 81458 recording exhibits a ![][image7] decay time of approximately ![][image8], characterized by a broad, persistent metallic body that sustains well above the low-frequency gesture.1 In contrast, the ReferenceSpringEngine imposes heavily damped discrete decay coefficients, resulting in a global ![][image7] of approximately ![][image9].1 By artificially dampening the resonators to conceal the lack of natural, intermittent broadband excitation, the current architecture isolates the macroscopic spring motion from the audible modal bank.  
To resolve this discrepancy, the physical model must transition from a smoothly coupled, continuous nonlinear oscillator to a piecewise or discontinuously excited system. The repeated acoustic articulation is the consequence of a low-frequency, dynamically shifted macroscopic oscillator causing intermittent, violent structural collisions—specifically coil clashing or geometric stiffness discontinuities—at its center-crossings or points of maximum deflection. This intermittent mechanical collision acts as a physical gate, periodically injecting broadband kinetic energy into a deeply resonant, high-Q modal bank that forms the persistent metallic continuous wave medium.

## **Physical Interpretation of the Target Acoustic System**

The recognizable deep, periodically articulated sound of a struck helical spring doorstop is a complex superposition of distributed wave propagation, lumped-parameter structural dynamics, and geometric intermittent contact.3 A rigorous physical interpretation must cleanly decouple these mechanisms and assign accurate terminology to each measured phenomenon.

### **Important Terminological Distinctions**

To avoid the conflation of mechanisms observed in previous development cycles 1, the following strict definitions are established:

> 1. **The slow macroscopic bend frequency:** This is the physical rate at which the entire spring structure swings back and forth. Stroboscopic observations place this between ![][image13] and ![][image14].3  
> 2. **The rate of center crossings:** As the spring swings, it crosses its neutral equilibrium point twice per full cycle. If the bend frequency is ![][image17], the center crossing rate is exactly ![][image1].  
> 3. **The rate of audible amplitude or energy lobes:** This matches the ![][image1] rate.1 It is the acoustic consequence of a physical event occurring twice per macroscopic cycle.  
> 4. **The perceived pitched fundamental:** This is a psychoacoustic phenomenon, usually mapped to the lowest persistent, high-Q resonant mode, measured here at ![][image18].1 It must not be confused with the macroscopic bend.  
> 5. **Higher resonant carrier modes:** The inharmonic peaks at ![][image3], ![][image4], ![][image5], and ![][image6] representing structural standing waves in the wire.1  
> 6. **Initial impact noise:** The broad, chaotic acoustic radiation generated strictly in the first ![][image19] of the physical strike.  
> 7. **Intermittent contact or collision:** The physical mechanism by which adjacent coils clash together under extreme compression, or where the restoring force becomes discontinuous.

### **The Dynamically Shifted Oscillator and Intermittent Excitation**

The physical source of the repeated energy transfer is not a smooth Duffing nonlinearity, but rather a phenomenon accurately described in nonlinear physics as the "dynamically shifted oscillator".7 When the spring is struck sideways, it undergoes a large-deflection transverse bending mode.5 Because the spring is a helix of finite wire thickness, the coils on the inner radius of the bend compress toward one another. Once the adjacent coils make physical contact, the spring can no longer compress locally; the structural stiffness becomes instantly discontinuous.  
The differential equation governing the dynamically shifted oscillator includes a Hooke's law restoring force plus a stiffness force that depends entirely upon the sign or threshold of the displacement, mathematically represented by terms such as ![][image20].7 In the physical doorstop, this sudden geometric stiffening, or direct metal-on-metal coil clash, acts as a shockwave generator.5 It produces an impulsive acceleration spike exactly twice per full oscillation cycle. Therefore, the ![][image1] acoustic lobe rate 1 is the direct result of an underlying ![][image17] macroscopic transverse bend repeatedly driving the structure into its discontinuous stiffness threshold. This mechanism explains why adding a generic amplitude envelope to a resonator is physically inadequate: an amplitude envelope merely turns the volume down, whereas the dynamically shifted oscillator physically injects new high-frequency kinetic energy into the system at every collision, sustaining the metallic body and generating the characteristic "sizzle."

### **Dispersive Wave Propagation in the Metallic Carrier**

While the macroscopic swing governs the timing of the articulation, the spectral makeup of the persistent metallic body is governed by the internal wave mechanics of the helical wire. The modes at ![][image2], ![][image3], ![][image4], ![][image5], and ![][image6] 1 are not harmonics of the transverse bend. Instead, they represent flexural and torsional waves traveling along the uncoiled length of the wire.4  
Helical springs are highly dispersive acoustic mediums. Dispersion implies that the phase velocity of a wave depends on its frequency; high-frequency transients travel faster through the wire than low-frequency waves. When the broadband impulse generated by the coil clash is injected into the wire, the wave disperses as it reflects between the rubber tip and the rigid wall mount. This dispersion produces a dense, inharmonic modal structure that decays very slowly, accounting for the ![][image21] ![][image7] decay.1 The physical model must therefore synthesize the continuous ringing of these dispersive waves while gating their excitation via the low-frequency dynamically shifted oscillator.

## **Recommended Minimal Architecture**

The evidence strictly dictates the selection of **Rank 1: Hybrid Lumped-Parameter Macroscopic Oscillator Exciting a Persistent Modal Bank**.  
This architecture represents the absolute simplest and most stable formulation capable of decoupling the low-frequency physical gesture from the high-frequency modal decay. By isolating the macroscopic oscillator and utilizing it strictly as a nonlinear *excitation source* rather than a direct audio generator, the parallel modal bank can be tuned to the precise empirical ![][image7] decay time of ![][image8] without simultaneously muddying the low-end spectrum or masking the sharp ![][image1] structural articulation.1  
To circumvent the "artificial tinny-metal character" noted in previous revisions 1, the modal bank must be restricted to a minimal, curated set of defining structural peaks (e.g., ![][image50] to ![][image51] modes). Because the system injects a broadband derivative impulse ![][image27] into these modes rather than a sterile digital Dirac impulse, the modes will ring with a complex, noisy initial transient that naturally mimics the physical dispersion of the metal structure. This interaction guarantees the synthesis of a broad metallic body rather than thin, isolated sinusoidal ringing, directly answering the central research question.

## **System-Identification Procedure**

To systematically extract the exact parameters from the 81458 recording 1 and accommodate future physical recordings, the following reproducible digital signal processing workflow is required. This procedure guarantees objective extraction of parameters and explicitly avoids the common pitfall of optimizing only a single scalar spectral distance, which often results in statically accurate but dynamically lifeless models.

### **Step 1: Strike Segmentation and Alignment**

Recordings containing multiple strikes must be segmented without confusing internal amplitude lobes for new strikes. Apply a nonlinear energy operator, such as the Teager-Kaiser Energy Operator (TKEO), to the raw audio to detect regions of impulsive energy independent of low-frequency sway. Identify the absolute maximum onset peak of the TKEO output and define this sample index as ![][image52]. Isolate a ![][image53] window relative to this onset to guarantee the capture of the full ![][image54] ![][image7] decay profile.1

### **Step 2: Macroscopic Motion Isolation and Lobe Timing**

To measure the macroscopic bend without interference from the metallic carrier, apply a steep 4th-order Linkwitz-Riley low-pass filter with a cutoff frequency of ![][image55]. Locate the zero-crossings of this filtered low-frequency signal. The instantaneous lobe rate is defined as the inverse of the time difference between consecutive zero-crossings. Track this trajectory across the first ![][image56] of the decay to quantify the nonlinear pitch glide (e.g., observing if the physical bend drops from an initial high-energy ![][image14] state down to a resting ![][image13] state).3

### **Step 3: Radiation-Envelope Extraction**

To confirm the exact timing of the energy transfer into the higher modes, apply a ![][image57] high-pass filter to the aligned recording to isolate the metallic body. Compute the analytical signal using a Hilbert transform and extract the absolute magnitude envelope. Calculate the autocorrelation of this envelope in moving ![][image58] Hanning windows. The first non-zero autocorrelation peak definitively confirms the exact periodic energy transfer rate, isolating the ![][image1] lobe phenomenon from the fundamental bend.1

### **Step 4: Persistent Spectral Peak Estimation**

To estimate the persistent modal frequencies, compute a heavily windowed averaged FFT (Welch's method, using ![][image59]\-sample frames and a Hann window) exclusively over the ![][image60] to ![][image61] region. Skipping the first ![][image62] avoids the chaotic initial strike transient, ensuring that only the truly persistent standing waves are identified. Extract the dominant peaks using standard peak-picking algorithms, targeting the empirically established ![][image63], and ![][image6] bins.1

### **Step 5: Damping (![][image7]) Estimation per Mode**

Apply narrow infinite impulse response (IIR) band-pass filters centered precisely on the extracted spectral peaks. Perform Schroeder integration on the squared output of each band-passed signal to yield a smooth, monotonically decreasing energy decay curve. Perform linear regression exclusively on the ![][image64] to ![][image65] region of the Schroeder curve to estimate the ![][image7] for each individual mode. This regression technique guarantees that periodic envelope troughs do not prematurely truncate the decay slope calculations.

## **Implementation Design**

The intended implementation environment is a VCV Rack modular plugin written in C++.1 Consequently, memory allocation must occur strictly during module instantiation. Furthermore, per-sample audio processing operations must completely bypass expensive \<cmath\> transcendental function calls, such as sin, cos, exp, and pow, inside the inner DSP loop.1 The design prioritizes fixed-size arrays, precomputed coefficient tables, and conditional block processing.

### **State Variables and Data Structures**

The system memory is divided into macroscopic state variables and a structured array for the modal filters.

C++  
// Macroscopic Oscillator State  
float mac\_x \= 0.0f;      // Current physical displacement  
float mac\_v \= 0.0f;      // Current physical velocity  
float prev\_force \= 0.0f; // Previous contact force (for derivative excitation)

// Modal Bank State (Fixed-size array for M=8 modes)  
struct ModeState {  
    float y1 \= 0.0f; // Unit delay z^-1  
    float y2 \= 0.0f; // Unit delay z^-2  
};  
ModeState modes;

// Precomputed DSP Coefficients (Updated only at control-rate)  
float mac\_omega\_sq;   
float mac\_damping;  
float contact\_stiffness \= 25000.0f;  
float contact\_gap \= 0.45f;  
float mode\_a1;  // Denominator coefficient 1  
float mode\_a2;  // Denominator coefficient 2  
float mode\_b0;  // Numerator gain coefficient

### **Coefficient Calculations and Sample-Rate Handling**

The modal bank utilizes a direct-form II transposed recursive topology, chosen for its excellent numerical properties regarding quantization noise in 32-bit floating-point arithmetic. The coefficients a1, a2, and b0 must be precomputed exclusively at the control rate, or whenever the host sample rate changes (e.g., from ![][image82] to ![][image35]).1

### **C++ DSP Pseudocode (Per-Sample Loop)**

The following continuous loop leverages Symplectic Euler integration. This semi-implicit method inherently preserves the Hamiltonian phase space of the continuous oscillator, guaranteeing stability without requiring expensive Runge-Kutta evaluation stages.

C++  
void process(float\* output, int num\_samples, float strike\_input) {  
    const float dt \= sample\_time; // e.g., 1.0f / 48000.0f  
      
    for (int i \= 0; i \< num\_samples; \++i) {  
        // 1\. Process Macroscopic Oscillator (Symplectic Euler)  
        mac\_v \+= strike\_input;   
          
        // 2\. Calculate dynamically shifted discontinuous contact force  
        float f\_contact \= 0.0f;  
        if (mac\_x \> contact\_gap) {  
            f\_contact \= contact\_stiffness \* (mac\_x \- contact\_gap);  
        } else if (mac\_x \< \-contact\_gap) {  
            f\_contact \= contact\_stiffness \* (mac\_x \+ contact\_gap);  
        }  
          
        // 3\. Compute total restoring force and update physics  
        float f\_total \= (mac\_omega\_sq \* mac\_x) \+ f\_contact;  
        mac\_v \-= dt \* (f\_total \+ mac\_damping \* mac\_v);  
        mac\_x \+= dt \* mac\_v; // Implicit velocity usage guarantees stability  
          
        // 4\. Generate Excitation Signal (Derivative of contact force)  
        // This generates impulsive broadband energy exclusively during collision  
        float excitation \= (f\_contact \- prev\_force) \* (1.0f / dt);  
        prev\_force \= f\_contact;  
          
        // Scale excitation to prevent numerical blowup  
        excitation \*= 0.0001f;   
          
        // 5\. Process Modal Bank (Highly Vectorizable Loop)  
        float out\_mix \= 0.0f;  
        for (int m \= 0; m \< 8; \++m) {  
            float y0 \= (mode\_b0\[m\] \* excitation)   
                     \- (mode\_a1\[m\] \* modes\[m\].y1)   
                     \- (mode\_a2\[m\] \* modes\[m\].y2);  
                       
            out\_mix \+= y0;  
              
            // Shift delay states  
            modes\[m\].y2 \= modes\[m\].y1;  
            modes\[m\].y1 \= y0;  
        }  
          
        // 6\. Subnormal mitigation and output clamping  
        // Prevent denormal CPU spikes  
        if (std::abs(out\_mix) \< 1e-15f) out\_mix \= 0.0f;  
          
        // Fast polynomial clip bounds to \+/- 5V for VCV Rack  
        output\[i\] \= fast\_polynomial\_clip(out\_mix \* 5.0f);   
    }  
}

### **Numerical Safeguards, Energy Bounds, and Retrigger Behavior**

To ensure the physical model remains bounded under violent bipolar, high-frequency retriggering (a common occurrence in modular synthesis environments):

> 1. **Velocity Saturation:** The incoming strike\_input is clamped prior to integration using a fast polynomial approximation mapped to a predefined energyCeiling. This maintains stability without the immense CPU cost of calling std::tanh per sample.1  
> 2. **Symplectic Stability:** The semi-implicit nature of updating mac\_v followed immediately by updating mac\_x guarantees integration stability even at the maximum ![][image35] limit.  
> 3. **Low-Cost Recovery and Sleep:** To conserve CPU overhead, track the total system energy ![][image88]. If ![][image89] and the absolute values of the modal bank states fall below ![][image90] for ![][image91] continuously 1, the engine sets a sleep flag, bypasses the DSP evaluation loop entirely, zeroes the output buffer, and resets all ![][image92] and ![][image93] memory states to exact zero to purge residual subnormal floats.
